title: Configuration Backup
levelTitle: Level 28 - Cisco IOS and IOS XE

cards.a: Copying the running or startup config to external storage (TFTP, SCP, FTP, or USB) or using the archive feature, and restoring it later. A backup is only useful if you can restore it.

cards.q: What should you back up for disaster recovery?
cards.a: The running-config (system:running-config) and the startup-config (nvram:startup-config), plus the IOS image stored on flash; the archive feature keeps automatic snapshots.

cards.q: Which commands copy the running-config to an external target?
cards.a: copy running-config tftp:, copy running-config scp:, copy running-config ftp:, copy running-config usb0:, or copy run flash:config.bak for a local flash copy.

cards.q: How does the archive feature provide versioned backups?
cards.a: archive enters archive mode; path sets the destination (for example tftp://...), write-memory forces an auto-save, maximum 14 keeps 14 versions, and show archive lists the saved snapshots.

cards.q: How do you restore a config from a server, from startup-config, or from an archive?
cards.a: copy tftp: running-config restores from a server, copy start run restores the saved config, configure replace file: applies an archived config, and copy flash: running-config restores a flash copy.

cards.q: How is archive version management controlled?
cards.a: maximum sets how many versions are kept, archives are numbered with timestamps in the names, and show archive config differences shows changes between configurations.

cards.q: What are the best practices for configuration backup?
cards.a: Schedule backups with automation, keep copies off-box so they survive device loss, verify backups by comparing hashes, and document the restore steps.

cards.q: Why is copy running-config startup-config not an off-box backup?
cards.a: It writes the config only to NVRAM on the same device, so it survives a reload but not device loss or hardware failure. Real disaster recovery requires copying the config off the device.

cards.q: A backup copy to a server fails. What do you check first?
cards.a: Reachability to the target, for example ping the TFTP or SCP server, plus free space on the destination and the correct file path.
